questions.title: Sneha's goal
questions.scenario: Sneha, a final-year BCom student in Kochi, writes down her goal for the term: “Get a good job.”
questions.question: Which rewrite turns it into a real goal?
options: “Work really hard this term and get a good job by the end.”
“Think every day about the job I want and how to get it.”
“Apply to 10 accounts internships by 30 November.”
“Get a better job than most of my classmates will get.”
questions.explanation: A real goal says what, how you’ll measure it, and by when: 10 applications, accounts internships, by 30 November.
questions.why_wrong: Working hard can’t be checked; thinking about a job isn’t an action you can measure; beating classmates depends on them, not on what you do.
questions.learning_outcome: A goal needs a what, a measure and a date.

questions.title: The big goal
questions.scenario: Arjun wants to pass his CA Foundation exam in June. It is now January, and he doesn’t know what to do on Monday.
questions.question: What should he do first?
options: Work back from June into monthly milestones, then this week’s tasks
Wait until he feels motivated, then study hard for a few weeks
Buy every recommended book first, so nothing is missing later on
Study whichever subject feels easiest that day, to build momentum
questions.explanation: Working backwards from the finish line gives milestones, then actions for this week. If he can’t say what he’ll do on Monday, the goal is still too big.
questions.why_wrong: Motivation is unreliable and leaves no plan; buying books isn’t a plan; picking the easiest subject skips the hard ones that need the most time.
questions.learning_outcome: Split a big goal into milestones and this week’s actions.

questions.title: Email to the manager
questions.scenario: Priya needs her internship manager to approve her leave for Friday. Her manager reads dozens of emails a day.
questions.question: How should her email start?
options: “I hope you are well. As you know, this has been a busy month for the team…”
“I wanted to talk to you about something important when you have a free moment.”
“Sorry to disturb you again, I know you are very busy with the new client this week.”
“Could you approve my leave this Friday, 8 March? Reasons and cover plan below.”
questions.explanation: Busy readers read the first line. Putting the request and the date first means the manager can say yes without digging.
questions.why_wrong: A long warm-up hides the request; asking to talk later adds a step; an apology fills the first line without saying what she needs.
questions.learning_outcome: Put what you want first, then the reasons.

questions.title: Getting a reply
questions.scenario: Rahul sends his project group a draft presentation and wants comments before Thursday’s class.
questions.question: Which closing line is most likely to get the replies he needs?
options: “Let me know your thoughts on any of the slides whenever you get a chance.”
“Could each of you check your own slides and reply by Wednesday 6 pm?”
“Feedback is welcome from everyone, as always. Thanks so much, everyone!”
“Hope the whole presentation looks good to everyone in the group.”
questions.explanation: A specific next step, with who and by when, gets replies. Open-ended requests are easy to put off.
questions.why_wrong: “Whenever you get a chance” has no deadline; “feedback is welcome” asks nobody for anything; hoping it looks good doesn’t ask for anything at all.
questions.learning_outcome: End with a specific ask and a date.

questions.title: The stalled fest
questions.scenario: Two weeks before the college fest, nobody has booked the sound system. Meera is a volunteer, not on the committee.
questions.question: What would leadership look like from Meera?
options: Wait for the committee to notice, since it isn’t her role
Tell everyone the fest will fail unless someone acts soon
Offer to get three quotes by Friday and ask who wants to help
Complain to the faculty adviser that the committee is careless
questions.explanation: Leadership without a title is noticing what isn’t getting done, taking it on, and making it easy for others to join.
questions.why_wrong: Waiting leaves the gap open; warning people without acting adds worry, not progress; complaining blames people instead of fixing the problem.
questions.learning_outcome: You can lead by taking on what isn’t being done.

questions.title: After the presentation
questions.scenario: Karthik led his group’s client presentation. The client loved the research, which Divya did, but the budget slide, which Karthik made, had an error.
questions.question: What should Karthik say to the team afterwards?
options: Thank Divya by name for the research, and own the budget mistake himself
Thank everyone in general, and not mention the budget slide again to anyone
Point out that the budget numbers came late from the finance student
Say the client was happy, so nothing else needs to be discussed
questions.explanation: Name the people who did the work when it goes well; own your part first when it doesn’t. It builds trust.
questions.why_wrong: General thanks miss Divya’s work and hiding the error stops anyone learning; blaming someone else damages trust; ignoring the error means it can happen again.
questions.learning_outcome: Share the credit, own the mistakes.

questions.title: The college app
questions.scenario: A student team has eight weeks to build a canteen-ordering app. One member suggests planning every detail now and building it all in week eight.
questions.question: What is the agile way to work?
options: Plan every detail now, so that nothing needs to change in the later weeks
Let each member build their part alone and join them at the end
Start with the hardest feature and leave testing for the last week
Build in two-week cycles, show a small working part each time, and adjust
questions.explanation: Short cycles mean you finish something small, see what happens, and learn sooner when a plan turns out wrong.
questions.why_wrong: A fixed eight-week plan finds problems too late; joining parts at the end hides problems until it’s too late; leaving testing to the end means late surprises.
questions.learning_outcome: Work in short cycles and learn from each one.

questions.title: End of the sprint
questions.scenario: At the end of a two-week sprint, Fatima’s team finished half of what they planned because two tasks were bigger than expected.
questions.question: What should the team do next?
options: Work weekends during the next sprint so the team can catch up on everything
Hold a retro: what went well, what didn’t, one change; then re-order the backlog
Drop the backlog and let each member decide their own tasks every morning
Plan exactly the same amount next sprint, and ask everyone to try harder
questions.explanation: A retrospective finds one thing to change, and the backlog is re-ordered as the team learns. Here, splitting big tasks smaller is a likely change.
questions.why_wrong: Weekend work hides the planning problem; dropping the backlog loses the priorities; planning the same amount repeats the mistake.
questions.learning_outcome: Look back, change one thing, re-order the backlog.

questions.title: The presentation
questions.scenario: After a nervous seminar presentation, Ananya says: “I’m just bad at presenting.”
questions.question: Which thought shows a growth mindset?
options: “Some people are born speakers, and I’m simply not one of them, sadly.”
“I’ll avoid presentations from now on and offer to do the written parts.”
“I’m not good at presenting yet. Next time I’ll practise it twice aloud.”
“It went badly because the audience wasn’t really interested in my topic.”
questions.explanation: “Not good at it yet” leaves room to improve and points to what to practise.
questions.why_wrong: “Born speakers” is a fixed verdict; avoiding presentations stops the skill growing; blaming the audience skips what she could change.
questions.learning_outcome: Skills grow with practice: add “yet”.

questions.title: The rejection
questions.scenario: Vikram was rejected after an interview. The recruiter said his answers were “too general”.
questions.question: What is the most useful next step?
options: Ask for an example of a general answer, then prepare specific stories
Decide that interviews favour confident people, and stop applying for a while
Apply to many more jobs quickly, so that a single rejection matters a lot less
Write to the recruiter explaining why his answers were actually detailed enough
questions.explanation: A rejection is information about what he did, not who he is. Asking for something specific and acting on it is how feedback teaches.
questions.why_wrong: Giving up turns one result into a verdict; more applications with the same answers repeat the problem; defending the answers ignores the feedback.
questions.learning_outcome: Treat setbacks as information and act on feedback.

questions.title: Finding a strength
questions.scenario: Rohan is asked to name a real strength for his internship application.
questions.question: Which is the best way to find one?
options: Choose whichever skill employers mention most often in the job ads he reads
Pick the subject he got his highest marks in, whatever he thinks of it
Ask a few friends to list his strengths and copy the longest list they give
Notice what he finds easy that friends find hard, and loses track of time doing
questions.explanation: A strength is something you do well that also gives you energy: what comes easily and absorbs you.
questions.why_wrong: A skill from job ads may not be his; marks alone don’t show what energises him; a friend’s list is a start but can’t replace his own noticing.
questions.learning_outcome: Strengths are what you do well and enjoy doing.

questions.title: The last-minute panic
questions.scenario: Every time a deadline is two days away, Isha panics and stops working well. She has three deadlines next month.
questions.question: What does knowing this trigger let her do?
options: Accept that panic is just part of her personality and can’t really change
Plan to finish each piece three days early, so the trigger never arrives
Avoid choosing courses with tight deadlines in all her future terms
Ask her teachers to remove or extend the deadlines just for her
questions.explanation: Knowing your triggers lets you plan around them instead of being caught out every time.
questions.why_wrong: Accepting it as fixed changes nothing; avoiding deadlines isn’t possible at work; asking to remove deadlines doesn’t help her manage them.
questions.learning_outcome: Know what throws you, and plan around it.

questions.title: A friend’s bad news
questions.scenario: Your friend tells you she didn’t get into the MBA programme she wanted. She is still talking about it.
questions.question: What does empathy look like here?
options: Tell her about the time you were rejected too, so she feels less alone
Quickly list three other good programmes she could apply to instead
Listen to the end, then say “That sounds really disappointing”
Tell her it wasn’t a great programme anyway, so she’s lucky
questions.explanation: Empathy starts with listening to the end and showing you heard the feeling, not just the facts.
questions.why_wrong: Your own story moves the focus to you; solutions too early skip what she feels; dismissing the programme dismisses her disappointment.
questions.learning_outcome: Listen to understand, and name the feeling.

questions.title: The angry customer
questions.scenario: During your internship at a bank branch, a customer is angry that his loan is taking weeks. You can’t speed it up.
questions.question: What is the empathetic response?
options: “Waiting weeks without news is frustrating. Let me check where it stands.”
“That’s just the bank’s process, sir, and I’m afraid I can’t change it.”
“You’re right, sir, the bank is very slow and badly run these days.”
“Please calm down, sir; every customer has to wait the same amount of time.”
questions.explanation: You can understand his frustration without agreeing that the bank is wrong, then do what you can.
questions.why_wrong: Quoting the process ignores how he feels; agreeing that the bank is badly run isn’t empathy, it’s taking sides; telling someone to calm down rarely calms them.
questions.learning_outcome: Show you understand, even when you can’t agree or fix it.

questions.title: The forwarded message
questions.scenario: A WhatsApp forward says a government scholarship gives ₹50,000 to every student who fills a form at a link.
questions.question: What should you ask first?
options: How many people have already shared it in other groups
Whether the message looks official and has the national emblem
Whether your friends have already filled the form in and got the money
Who sent it out, how they know, and what they gain if you fill the form
questions.explanation: Ask where it came from, what evidence backs it, and what the sender gains. Check on the official government site, not the link.
questions.why_wrong: Many shares don’t make it true; logos are easy to copy; friends filling it in only spreads the risk.
questions.learning_outcome: Check who says so, and how they know.

questions.title: The course decision
questions.scenario: Nikhil is sure a ₹1.5 lakh data science course will get him a job, because its website shows 98% placement.
questions.question: What would test his view most fairly?
options: Read more of the success stories on the course’s own website before paying
Ask recent students, and check what the course counts as “placed”
Ask the course counsellor whether the course is really worth the fees
Trust the number, since 98% placement is far higher than most courses
questions.explanation: A strong view survives its best counter-argument. Independent students and a clear definition of “placed” test the claim.
questions.why_wrong: More success stories from the same source only confirm the view; the counsellor gains from his enrolment; a high number proves nothing without knowing how it was counted.
questions.learning_outcome: Test your view against the best case against it.

questions.title: Fundraising ideas
questions.scenario: Your NSS unit needs ₹20,000 for a village library. The first idea, a bake sale, raises too little.
questions.question: What should the group do in its next meeting?
options: Vote straight away between the bake sale and doing nothing at all
Ask the most senior member to choose the best idea alone, to save time
List lots of ideas in ten minutes without judging, then pick the best
Copy exactly what last year’s unit did, since that plan worked for them
questions.explanation: Good ideas usually come after many ordinary ones. Generate first, judge later.
questions.why_wrong: Voting on one idea skips better ones; one person choosing loses the group’s ideas; last year’s plan may not fit this goal.
questions.learning_outcome: Generate many ideas before you judge them.

questions.title: The empty library
questions.scenario: Few students use the college library in the evenings. The librarian asks for a fresh idea.
questions.question: Which approach best uses “borrow and combine”?
options: Ask what makes cafés busy in the evening, and try that in the library
Make a new rule that every student must visit the library twice a week
Repaint the library in bright colours and hope more students come in
Run a survey asking students to rate the library from 1 to 5
questions.explanation: Most new ideas take something that works in one place and use it in another, like a café’s good seating, snacks or group tables.
questions.why_wrong: A rule forces visits without making the library better; repainting is a guess with no reason behind it; a 1-to-5 rating doesn’t produce ideas.
questions.learning_outcome: Borrow what works elsewhere and combine it.

questions.title: Two offers
questions.scenario: Aisha has two internship offers: a known brand with no stipend, and a small startup paying ₹12,000 a month. She keeps going round in circles.
questions.question: What should she do?
options: Choose whichever offer her friends and family say sounds more impressive
Wait until one of the companies withdraws its offer, then take the other
Accept both offers now and decide later which one to leave
Write down each option and what it would lead to, then choose and note why
questions.explanation: Listing the options and their consequences, then choosing and saying why, beats going round in circles.
questions.why_wrong: Friends don’t carry the consequences; waiting may lose both offers; accepting both and leaving one breaks a promise.
questions.learning_outcome: Write the options and their consequences, then choose.

questions.title: Not enough information
questions.scenario: Dev must choose his final-year elective by Friday. He can’t find out everything about both options in time.
questions.question: What is the best way to decide?
options: Ask for an extension until he knows absolutely everything about both
Choose on what he knows by Friday, and note what to check later
Pick at random, since he can’t know everything about either one anyway
Choose whichever elective has the most students signed up for it
questions.explanation: You rarely have all the information. Set a date, choose the best option you have, and review later what you learned.
questions.why_wrong: Waiting for complete information means never deciding; random choice ignores what he does know; class size says little about whether it suits him.
questions.learning_outcome: Decide on time with what you know, then review.

questions.title: Late every day
questions.scenario: Sana keeps arriving late to her 9 am internship. She asks herself why: she leaves late. Why? She wakes late. Why? She’s on her phone until 1 am.
questions.question: What should she fix first?
options: Take an auto instead of the bus every morning
Set three alarms for the morning
Stop using her phone after 11 pm
Apologise to her manager every time she is late
questions.explanation: Asking “why” more than once reaches a cause she can change: late-night phone use. The other fixes treat symptoms.
questions.why_wrong: A faster auto helps today but not the cause; more alarms fight the same late night; apologising doesn’t change anything.
questions.learning_outcome: Ask why until you reach a cause you can change.

questions.title: Low attendance
questions.scenario: Your coding club’s attendance dropped from 40 to 12. Members say the 7 pm timing clashes with dinner.
questions.question: What is the best next step?
options: Try a 5 pm session next week and count who comes
Redesign the whole club over the summer before changing anything
Ask the college to make attendance compulsory
Keep 7 pm, since changing it might upset the 12 who still come
questions.explanation: Break the fix into a small step you can test now. A trial at 5 pm shows quickly whether timing was the cause.
questions.why_wrong: A summer-long redesign delays any learning; compulsory attendance hides the real problem; keeping 7 pm ignores what members said.
questions.learning_outcome: Try a small fix and see what happens.

questions.title: A new team
questions.scenario: Zoya has joined a new internship team. She wants people to trust her.
questions.question: What builds that trust fastest?
options: Telling the team about her best marks and the awards she won in college
Agreeing with everyone in every meeting so that nobody is ever upset
Staying quiet in meetings until she has been there for a few months
Keeping small promises, thanking people and remembering what they tell her
questions.explanation: Trust is built in small moments: kept promises, thanks and remembering what people said.
questions.why_wrong: Talking about marks impresses but doesn’t build trust; agreeing with everything makes her views unknown; staying silent gives people nothing to trust.
questions.learning_outcome: Small, reliable actions build trust.

questions.title: The group project
questions.scenario: Your project partner keeps changing the slides you made without asking. It is starting to annoy you.
questions.question: What should you say?
options: “You always ruin my work. Stop touching my slides from now on, please.”
“When slides change without a word, I lose track. Can we agree how?”
Say nothing, and quietly change the slides back to yours each night
Complain to the teacher that your partner is very hard to work with
questions.explanation: Describe the problem and how it affects you, ask for their view, and look for an option that works for both. Disagree with the action, not the person.
questions.why_wrong: “Always” and “ruin” attack the person; changing slides back silently starts a hidden fight; going to the teacher first skips talking to your partner.
questions.learning_outcome: Disagree with the idea, not the person.

questions.title: Exam season
questions.scenario: Three weeks before exams, Kabir is sleeping badly, snapping at his family and scrolling instead of studying.
questions.question: What are these, most likely?
options: Signs he is lazy and needs more discipline
Normal behaviour that will go away on its own after exams
Early signs of stress he can act on now
Proof that he chose the wrong course
questions.explanation: Poor sleep, snapping and scrolling are common early signs of stress. Spotting them early lets him act sooner.
questions.why_wrong: Calling it laziness blames him instead of helping; waiting for exams to end lets it grow; one stressful month says nothing about his course.
questions.learning_outcome: Learn your early signs of stress.

questions.title: Too much to do
questions.scenario: Lakshmi has an assignment due tomorrow, a quiz on Friday, a family function and club work. She feels overwhelmed.
questions.question: What helps most?
options: Write everything down, do the assignment first, and plan a short break
Do a little of everything tonight so nothing is left untouched
Skip sleep tonight so that she can finish everything on the list
Wait until she feels less stressed before starting anything
questions.explanation: Write it all down, pick the one thing that matters most and do it first. Rest is part of the plan, not a reward.
questions.why_wrong: A little of everything finishes nothing; skipping sleep makes tomorrow worse; waiting to feel better delays the work that’s causing the stress.
questions.learning_outcome: Plan, prioritise, and build in rest.

questions.title: After the results
questions.scenario: Tanvi is upset after her semester results but can’t say why. She just feels “bad”.
questions.question: What would help her most first?
options: Distract herself with a film and not think about it
Tell herself to stop feeling bad because it won’t help
Compare her marks with friends to see if others did worse
Put the feeling into exact words, like “disappointed” or “worried”
questions.explanation: Naming a feeling exactly makes it easier to handle. “Name it to tame it.”
questions.why_wrong: Distraction postpones it; ordering herself not to feel bad rarely works; comparing marks usually adds feelings rather than easing them.
questions.learning_outcome: Name a feeling to manage it.

questions.title: The rude comment
questions.scenario: In the class WhatsApp group, someone mocks Farhan’s idea. He is angry and starts typing a sharp reply.
questions.question: What is the best thing to do?
options: Send the reply at once, so everyone sees he won’t be pushed around
Pause and wait an hour, then decide whether and how to reply
Leave the group straight away, so that it can’t happen again
Reply with a joke about the other person instead
questions.explanation: Between what happens and what you do, there is a moment. Waiting gives him room to choose a response instead of reacting.
questions.why_wrong: An instant angry reply is a reaction he may regret; leaving the group avoids it but loses the group; a mocking joke answers anger with more of it.
questions.learning_outcome: Pause before you respond.
